rewrites.summary:
Armenia demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised — Armenia has no anti-LGBT legislation of the restrictive type seen in neighbouring countries — and an administrative practice for legal gender recognition exists (medicalised). Pink Armenia’s 2024 annual report documents ongoing violations including inhuman/degrading treatment, and hate speech is routine in public discourse; the 2018 failed anti-discrimination bill means there is still no SOGI-specific (sexual orientation and gender identity) protection statute. The capital, Yerevan, has a small organised community (Pink Armenia and Right Side — a national rights organisation and a trans-led local group), but visibility carries real risk.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; social hostility significant outside central areas of the capital (Yerevan); police response unreliable; border and document-screening practice is not covered in the current sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent comparative material covering this nation and its two neighbours: the domestic legal baseline — decriminalisation (2003), legal gender change but surgery required since 2006, restricted gender-affirming care, no nonbinary recognition, “ambiguous” hate-crime protections since 2022, no SOGI (sexual orientation and gender identity) anti-discrimination protections (no protection statute), same-sex marriage banned — and very low public-opinion acceptance scores.

History and incidence: a 2009 fact-finding mission and 2012-era reporting document an earlier era’s societal and institutional hostility (including an arson attack on a community venue with a slow police response); a 2019 report documented legislators calling for a trans activist to be burned alive after a national-assembly speech.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The medicalised legal gender recognition practice and the absence of a SOGI protection statute are resident-facing; a visitor’s documents come from their home country.

Resident-facing data from the sources: the 2024 annual report documents discrimination, torture and inhuman/degrading treatment, violations of private and family life, education and work rights, and routine hate speech; a comparison service records very low public-opinion acceptance scores; the pressure episode around a trans individual in a beauty pageant is domestic media context.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Protection-statute absence and legal-gender-recognition medicalisation are resident-facing. The current sources do not describe border/document-screening practice for visitors, and the practical enforcement of “ambiguous” hate-crime protections is unquantified.

Unverified: the current administrative status of the medicalised recognition path, and whether it could apply to a visitor; the 2009 mission and 2012 report are dated context.

rewrites.summary:
Australia is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court’s landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW, another state, passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction; and marriage equality has held since 2017 (relevant to same-sex partners travelling together).

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS research documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent context: the national legal trend is settled and protective — federal sex-discrimination protection (2013), the 2024 federal court reading of it, and rapid state modernisation — while the live policy pressure documented nationally is the organised exclusionary campaign landscape (facilities and records-access disputes, rights-rollback pressures).

History and framing: state-by-state decriminalisation unfolded over decades from laws inherited from the historic metropole (one state kept the death penalty until 1949), and the national protections debate includes an ongoing terminological dispute over whether intersex people belong inside the same framework — framing, not visitor-facing risk. A federal hate-crime offence (2025) and conversion-therapy bans covering most of the population (2024) extend the protective layer beyond the earlier baseline.
rewrites.localsOnly:
State-level legal gender recognition remains a patchwork (only some jurisdictions are self-declaration) and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing.

Resident-facing discrimination data from the sources: a 2003 research brief documented trans people’s difficulties with sex designations on identity documents (passports, licences and birth certificates), high job-loss rates around transition, and greater exposure to assault and harassment in public places; the 2024 state-law modernisations (Queensland, NSW) govern residents, not visitors.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
State-level legal gender recognition patchwork and healthcare access gaps are resident-facing; the current sources do not assess marriage or partner-travel questions beyond the 2017 marriage-equality baseline, and border-document screening practice for visitors is not detailed.

Unverifiable in the current sources: three of the seven listed sources were not retrievable at research time (access denied; page removed; assembly bill text), including the 2024 discrimination ruling report and a state bill text; the remaining assessment of organised campaigns rests on the research brief alone.

rewrites.summary:
Azerbaijan is dangerous for trans visitors. The documented pattern is grim: a trans woman was tortured and murdered in the capital, Baku, in July 2023; a second trans woman’s murder in March 2024 was met with a police response lacking comprehensive investigation; several other trans people were physically assaulted, including by police themselves; and two trans women were detained for “hooliganism” for making noise. Government-affiliated media air targeted discriminatory hate speech.

Nothing formally criminalises gender expression, but police are perpetrators rather than protectors, and the state is one of the world’s more closed authoritarian systems — there is no recourse and no community infrastructure that can operate openly. An April 2024 ECtHR ruling (the regional rights-court) found violations in Azerbaijan’s treatment of LGBTI applicants.

For a visitor: no statute bars entry or expression, but discovery risks police abuse with no remedy, and the murder-impunity pattern is documented; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Historical backdrop: the current enforcement pattern follows documented precedent — a September 2017 wave of police raids in the capital detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges with beatings documented (part of arrests ahead of an international sporting event), and a 2017-era shadow report to an international women’s-rights committee documented government-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, forced marriages, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women, with a local organisation serving hundreds of LBT people.

Litigation and monitoring: an April 2024 regional-court ruling found violations in the country’s treatment of LGBTI applicants (the underlying 2017 arrests acknowledged by the state in 2019); media monitoring found 77% of analysed media pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The economic marginalisation data (black-market work, precarious housing), the refusals in employment and housing, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women are resident-facing; the police-perpetrator pattern is traveler-relevant.

Resident-facing from the sources: the economic exclusion profile (a trans woman denied housing and employment after her trans-inclusive employer shut down), a family forcibly transporting a young woman to the capital after she came out, and the 2017 raid wave affecting residents; the shadow report to an international women’s-rights committee documents government-approved ignorance and forced marriages.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Economic exclusion data is resident-facing; the police-perpetrator pattern is traveler-relevant. The current sources do not detail border/document-screening practice for visitors, and the specific identity-document impossibility is a resident administrative matter.

Unverified: whether foreign visitors are at the same risk of police attention as residents, and the current enforcement trajectory of the 2024 ruling; the 2017-era reports are dated context.

rewrites.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised; the capital Sarajevo’s Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 with heavy (necessary) police protection; and most cantons have now appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes — genuine institutional progress.

Counterweights from the 2024 Pink Report (the annual monitor): negative events are accumulating, the trend is unfavourable outside Sarajevo (especially in one internal region, Republika Srpska), and trans people occupy a “precarious position” — no legal gender recognition framework, restricted healthcare access, and institutional suspicion. The state is also deeply dysfunctional generally.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; stick to Sarajevo and tourist areas; avoid visible trans presentation in the hostile internal region (Republika Srpska) and rural areas. Marriage recognition is restricted to opposite-sex couples in the entities — relevant to same-sex partners travelling together; the border and document position for visitors is not detailed in the current sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent context: the legal baseline is entity-split — decriminalisation happened through the two internal regions’ own criminal codes (1996, 1998) and a state-level anti-discrimination law (2009, amended 2016 to add gender identity) — so the visitor’s protection depends on which internal region’s institutions respond; the state itself is deeply dysfunctional, which colours enforcement quality.

History and flux: a 2014 organised attack on Pride organisers, even with prior police coordination, is documented precedent; the 2024 report describes the negative trend as “becoming increasingly evident”.
rewrites.localsOnly:
No legal gender recognition framework and restricted healthcare access — resident-facing; the precarious position documented in the annual Pink Report describes residents’ situation.

Resident-facing from the sources: the legal gender recognition procedure is formally accessible but vague and ineffective in practice, conditioning document changes on ‘completed’ medical transition — described as discriminatory and degrading; the 2016 amendments and internal-region (entity) hate-crime regulations are domestic statutory facts.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Hostility varies by internal region (Republika Srpska is the documented hotspot); legal-gender-recognition absence is resident-facing; the current sources do not detail border/document-screening practice for visitors or the marriage question beyond the opposite-sex-only restriction.

Unverified: whether the 2024 negative trend has changed the visitor-facing safety picture since the report; the 2014 attack precedent is dated context.

rewrites.summary:
Canada is exceptionally safe for trans visitors — the strongest of the large Western countries. Gender identity and expression are protected grounds in the Canadian Human Rights Act and the Criminal Code’s hate-crime provisions (Bill C-16, 2017); most provinces offer self-declaration legal gender recognition; federal documents offer an X marker; and healthcare coverage is universal. There are no bathroom laws, no border friction (Canadian authorities have not issued or received trans-traveller warnings), and courts consistently enforce protections.

The counterweights are real but climate-level: police-reported hate crimes have risen six consecutive years (+169% since 2018), with gender identity/expression crimes among the fastest-growing categories; Egale documents a rising organised anti-trans movement; and Alberta/Saskatchewan have enacted resident-facing policy rollbacks (school pronoun and healthcare restrictions). A 2022 federal survey found 39% of 2SLGBTQI+ respondents experienced identity-based violence in five years — 90% of it verbal abuse, 17% physical.

For a visitor: full legal protection, functioning recourse, low probability of anything beyond verbal harassment in hostile pockets; the current sources report no marriage or partner-travel friction.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent climate: the 2017 protections were framed as national leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash, and the resident-facing provincial school-pronoun and healthcare rollbacks (Alberta, Saskatchewan) are the visible policy turbulence in an otherwise settled national framework.

No litigation flux is reported in the current sources: the 2012 human-rights shadow submission predates the 2017 protections (gender identity/expression added to the human-rights act and criminal code; conversion-therapy prohibitions from 2021/22) and is superseded.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Provincial self-declaration legal gender recognition, the federal X marker, and the Alberta/Saskatchewan school-pronoun and healthcare rollbacks are resident-facing; the 2022 survey data describes residents.

The current sources add resident-facing legal infrastructure: a 2016 provincial reform created a document-update pathway (self-declaration plus a doctor’s letter, the surgery requirement removed); provincial human-rights commission policy guidance supports sexual-orientation discrimination complaints; the 2012 shadow submission documented the era’s trans-protection gaps.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Provincial healthcare/school policy rollbacks are resident-facing climate signals; the current sources do not address marriage or partner-travel questions for a visitor in any detail.

Unverifiable in the current sources: the 2024 national hate-crime analysis page and the 2022 federal survey page were not retrievable at research time (redirect loop; timeout), so the figures above rest on the record’s summary text and the retrievable source claims.

A national newspaper (Jun 2017): the national legislative chamber passed the 2017 amendment by 67-11, prohibiting discrimination based on gender identity and gender expression and adding gender identity/expression to the criminal code hate-motivation provisions — framed as national leadership amid a global anti-LGBT backlash.

A local human-rights commission policy (Part I): legal context, case law and legislation for sexual-orientation discrimination complaints under the local human-rights code, which expressly covers gender identity and gender expression — official guidance a visitor or resident can invoke for discrimination recourse.

rewrites.summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors — and deteriorating fast. In September 2024 parliament (the elected national assembly) passed the law “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”: it bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, LGBT public assembly, and dissemination of LGBT information — the region’s harshest legislative package. One day after passage, Kesaria Abramidze, one of Georgia’s best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in the capital (Tbilisi); mourners and the news agency AP drew a direct line between the law’s rhetoric and the killing.

This compounds an existing pattern: the 2021 Pride office ransacking by far-right mobs while police stood by, the foreign-agents law choking local rights groups and LGBT NGOs (which refuse to register and face bankruptcy), and documented police failure to protect demonstrators (Identoba v. Georgia ECtHR line of cases before the regional human-rights court, still unimplemented). Georgia’s visible trans community is now legally erased and physically targeted.

For a visitor: being visibly trans in Georgia now carries both statutory risk (assembly/information provisions) and elevated street-violence risk, with police as unreliable protectors; border and document-screening practice is not covered by the current sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent context: the 2024 law is the harshest package of its kind in the region, framed in the style of a neighbouring nation’s legislation (the Russia-style ‘protecting family values’ model); the law drew international condemnation — the regional bloc’s officials and a foreign parliamentary committee chair warned it further derails the country’s membership path — while asylum-seeking by LGBTI people has risen.

Institutional backdrop: the foreign-agents law, separate from the family-values law, is choking rights organisations (fines and bankruptcy for those refusing to register), and the court line of cases on police failure to protect demonstrators remains unimplemented — backdrop, not visitor-facing statute.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The 2024 law’s legal-gender-recognition ban and transition-healthcare ban are resident-facing; its assembly/information provisions can reach visitors.

Resident-facing from the sources: the foreign-agents law’s threat of fines and bankruptcy to unregistered rights organisations, falling service applications, the flight and asylum documentation of large numbers of LGBTI people, and the 2012-era documentation of trans-specific legal barriers (no legal pathway to change official gender; paperwork mismatches affecting jobs).
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
The 2024 law’s healthcare and legal-gender-recognition provisions are resident-facing; its assembly/information provisions can reach visitors. The current sources do not detail border/document screening for visitors or whether the statutory assembly and information provisions have been enforced against individual travellers.

Unverified: the practical enforcement rate of the 2024 provisions on the street, and the current status of the unimplemented court rulings; the 2012 legal-barriers item predates the 2024 law.

News/advocacy report (May 2012): ‘laws discriminate on transgender rights’ — legal activists say the law should be changed to allow gender recognition; job applications become difficult when a person’s gender identity doesn’t match official paperwork — trans-specific legal barriers in this nation.

News report (Jun 2019): the interior ministry said holding the capital’s Pride was ‘impossible’ in the planned city-centre locations ‘due to safety risks’; organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart it — the nation’s first-ever Pride.

rewrites.summary:
North Macedonia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised, and the capital, Skopje, hosts both Pride and an organised Trans March for Visibility (TransFormA, March 2024) — public trans organising that proceeds without serious incident. Anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and gender identity (2019 amendments). There are no same-sex or equal marriage rights (the 2014 marriage-definition motion, defining marriage as a union of one man and one woman) — a consideration for partners travelling as a couple — and the Law on Civil Registry’s legal gender recognition chapter was withdrawn.

Counterweights: hate speech and hate crimes remain common with no effective justice-system response (European Commission), social-media death threats are routine, and the legal gender recognition absence is documented.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; small but functioning community; standard regional street-hostility caution; no marriage recognition for same-sex visiting couples and no local document-change pathway; border and document-screening practice is not covered in the current sources.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent context: the 2019 anti-discrimination amendment trend is offset by a justice-system non-response documented by regional monitors and the national government’s withdrawal of the legal-gender-recognition chapter from the civil-registry bill on the eve of committee review; an international rights index once ranked the country worst in its regional bloc (the only one in the worst tier), and a 2023 economic analysis quantified discrimination’s drag on national growth and jobs.
rewrites.localsOnly:
No legal gender recognition — resident-facing; the justice-system non-response affects resident victims.

Resident-facing from the sources: the hate-speech and hate-crime prevalence and the absence of effective response, the withdrawal of the civil-registry gender-recognition chapter, and the 2014 marriage-definition motion are all domestic legal and social facts; a 2019 human-rights report and the 2012 index document the resident situation.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Justice-system non-response and legal-gender-recognition absence are resident-facing/climate signals; the sources do not address visitor document screening or border treatment of trans travellers.

Unverified: whether the 2014 marriage-definition motion is current law (the sources only record its submission), and whether reported community events continue to proceed without serious incident.

News report (30 March 2024): a local trans group’s March for Visibility in the capital marked the international Transgender Day of Visibility — “we march bravely” — while noting a trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

A foreign affairs department’s 2019 human-rights report for this nation: official assessment including the sexual-orientation and gender-identity section — anti-discrimination law, societal violence and discrimination against LGBT persons.

News report (13 October 2023): economic analysis with local LGBTI groups quantifying how anti-LGBTQ discrimination harms the economies of this nation and a neighbouring one — discrimination cast as a measurable drag on growth and jobs, without country-specific figures in the piece.

News report (February 2012): an international rights index ranked this nation worst in its regional bloc on the graded scale — the only national record in the bloc in the worst tier of human-rights violations and discrimination.

News report (July 2014): the government submitted a constitutional motion defining marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman — ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption — needing two-thirds of legislative votes with conservative support expected.

rewrites.summary:
New Zealand is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration has been in force since 2023 (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act); the Law Commission reviewed Human Rights Act protections for trans, non-binary and intersex people in 2024; and takatāpui/rainbow communities have deep institutional recognition. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

The counterweights are documented and significant for the street climate: reports of gender-identity hate crimes jumped 42% between 2022 and 2023 (161 to 229 incidents), spiking around the Posie Parker visit (the visiting campaigner); the national survey (Counting Ourselves) found almost 1 in 5 trans and non-binary people were threatened with physical violence in four years, and 8% experienced it; and community advocates accuse police of failing rainbow communities amid far-right agitation (library events crashed, church arson threats).

For a visitor: full legal protection; moderate probability of harassment in charged spaces; functioning (if criticised) institutions.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Adjacent consolidation: the statutory wins named in the current sources (an ID-correction registration law easing document changes, and a conversion-practices prohibition) are recent and settled, so the visitor-facing floor is stable; the hate-incident spike and police-accountability debate are the live institutional flux around it.

History and comparisons: the local history materials record a long liberal-reform record (early women’s suffrage, decriminalisation, equal marriage among the first 13 countries worldwide, and a reported first for trans people in elected national office); an international travel index (2026) rates legal and living conditions across 18 categories and is aimed at travellers’ decisions.
rewrites.localsOnly:
The self-declaration legal gender recognition regime (2023) and the Law Commission review are resident-facing; the Counting Ourselves survey data describes residents.

Resident-facing from the sources: the police hate-incident data carries a documented undercount caveat, and the almost-one-in-five violence figures come from a community survey; a local community archive (over 1,000 audio recordings, a timeline, and reform-debate transcripts) documents institutional recognition and history.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes:
Counting Ourselves (resident-survey) data describes residents; healthcare gaps are resident-facing; marriage and partner-travel questions are not covered by the current sources (equal marriage has been legal in this nation since 2013, per the historical materials).

Unresolved: whether the documented 42% hate-incident increase translates into visitor-facing encounter rates; the community-archive source is context material with no risk finding for this record.
